html:
The Roanoke Colony was England's first attempt at a lasting settlement in North America, on Roanoke Island in what is now North Carolina. It was backed by Sir Walter Raleigh under a charter from Elizabeth I, and is remembered as the "Lost Colony".

A scouting voyage in 1584 met the Secotan and other Algonquian-speaking peoples of the sounds and brought two men, Manteo and Wanchese, to England. In 1585 a military outpost of about a hundred men under Ralph Lane landed on Roanoke Island, in the land of the Roanoke people. Lane explored north towards the Chesapeake and up the rivers to the Chowanoke and the Moratoc, hunting for copper and a passage west. Short of food, the colonists quarrelled with their hosts, and Lane killed the Roanoke leader Wingina in 1586. The men went home that year with Francis Drake.

The artist John White and the scientist Thomas Harriot of this first group left the best early record of the region's peoples, including the Weapemeoc.

In 1587 White brought back about 115 settlers, men, women and children; his granddaughter Virginia Dare was the first English child born in the Americas. White sailed home for supplies, but war with Spain kept him away. When he returned in 1590 the settlement was empty, with the word CROATOAN carved on a post. What happened to the settlers is unknown; many historians think some joined Native communities nearby. England tried again at Jamestown in Virginia in 1607.
